progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: a pathogen leaves one host, travels and enters the next (stations "leave", "travel", "enter"); modes of transmission (direct, indirect through objects, food, water or air, vectors); "Every control measure breaks a link"; the route board and its `BreakMark`. From b06: skin and mucus as barriers. From b09: vaccination gives memory cells. From g03: wound washing appeared in the Q3 stem. Not assumed: hygiene mechanism, environmental management, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, incubation period, biosecurity, herd immunity, R₀ (screen only), coverage.
progression.startsWith: Locate transmission links that controls can interrupt. The video opens: In 1847, a Vienna hospital had two maternity clinics.
progression.stopsAfter: reading Semmelweis's clinic data as evidence that hands carried the pathogen; locating the link each of four measures breaks (travel: hygiene; leave: isolation and quarantine; the next host: vaccination); explaining how soap and water remove microbes and why alcohol rub works less well against norovirus and bacterial spores; explaining environmental management (cleaning surfaces, cooking food, treating water, removing sewage) and its strength (works without anyone remembering); explaining why hygiene does little against an airborne pathogen such as measles; defining isolation (separating infected people) and its limit (spread before symptoms); defining contact tracing and quarantine (separating exposed people who aren't sick yet) and explaining why quarantine lasts about as long as the incubation period; describing border quarantine and biosecurity; explaining herd immunity (enough immune people, so each case infects fewer than one other on average; protects those who can't be vaccinated) and why more contagious diseases need higher coverage (measles about 93 per cent threshold, 95 per cent target) and why local coverage matters; evaluating measures by which link, speed, how long they can last, and cost, and justifying layered control.
progression.nextLesson: why antibiotics and antivirals work differently (route entry bio-m7-b11).

teaching.task: In 1847, washing hands in chlorine cut deaths in a maternity clinic, years before anyone accepted that germs cause disease. How do hygiene, isolation, quarantine and vaccination each break the chain of spread, and how do you judge which one works?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why handwashing cut deaths (hands were the travel link; the solution killed the bacteria; hook, 3); how soap works and why alcohol rub differs (3); why environmental management lasts (4); why hygiene fails for measles (the virus travels in air and lingers; 5); why isolation starts late (infectious before the rash; 6); why quarantine lasts about the incubation period (an infected contact shows symptoms within it; 7); why herd immunity stops chains and protects the unvaccinated (each case meets too few susceptible people; 9); why measles needs higher coverage (each case would infect about 15; 10); why measures are layered (each misses something; 11). Visible case: the same board gains one break per measure; the same timeline shows the isolation gap and the quarantine window. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 7 (tracing, quarantine, incubation, post-exposure) and 11 (criteria table) are the densest, so earlier brackets and rows dim.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In 1847 a Vienna hospital's doctors' clinic lost about one mother in ten to fever after birth while the midwives' clinic lost far fewer, and washing hands in chlorine cut the deaths years before germs were accepted, so the question is how hygiene, isolation, quarantine and vaccination each break the chain of spread and how to judge which one works. A pathogen has to leave one host, travel and enter a next host it can infect, and every control measure breaks a link. Handwashing broke the travel link carried by the doctors' hands, and environmental management (cleaning surfaces, cooking food, treating water and carrying sewage away) works on places. Hygiene cannot break an airborne route such as measles, so isolation keeps infected people away from others, but people can spread disease before symptoms, so contacts are traced and those not immune are quarantined for the incubation period; border quarantine keeps pests and diseases out. Vaccination removes hosts the pathogen can use, and when enough people are immune each case infects fewer than one other on average, so the chain dies out (herd immunity); a more contagious disease needs more people immune. Measures are judged by which link they break, how fast they work, how long they last and what they cost people, and the memory aid is isolate the infected, quarantine the exposed. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1847, a Vienna hospital had two maternity clinics. In the doctors' clinic, about one mother in ten died of a fever after giving birth. In the midwives' clinic, far fewer died. Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that the doctors came straight from autopsies. He made them wash their hands in a chlorine solution, and deaths fell to about the midwives' level. So how can washing, or keeping people apart, stop a disease nobody could see?

teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ4-02 (p 55): "investigate procedures that can be employed to prevent the spread of disease, including but not limited to: (ACSBL124)", with the listed items "hygiene practices", "quarantine" and "vaccination, including passive and active immunity (ACSBL100, ACSBL123)" (this video: hygiene, quarantine, and vaccination at population level as herd immunity; "public health campaigns" is touched by vaccination coverage only; "use of pesticides" and "genetic engineering" are b12). B7-IQ4-04 (p 55): "investigate and evaluate environmental management and quarantine methods used to control an epidemic or pandemic". Verb "investigate" (B7-IQ4-02): the hook reads Semmelweis's clinic data as evidence, and attempt 1 tests a quarantine plan against incubation data. Verb "evaluate" (B7-IQ4-04): scene 11 gives the four criteria and judges hygiene, environmental management, isolation and quarantine, and vaccination against them; attempt 1 is an evaluate item. Environmental management is taught as changing places (surfaces, food, water, sewage) so the pathogen can't reach new hosts (scene 4); border quarantine for an epidemic or pandemic is scene 8.

design.visualSystem: One control board, b03's route chain board extended: two coded host circles (b03's `HostCircles` style; abstract, never people), "infected host" at the left and "new host" at the right, with b03's three stations "leave", "travel", "enter" and a fourth small station after "enter", "can it be infected?" (added in scene 2). Each control lands at its station as a painted plate plus b03's coded `BreakMark` (a short scribble cut across the lane): hygiene at "travel", isolation at "leave", quarantine at "leave" (dashed, because the exposed host may or may not be infected), vaccination at "can it be infected?". Scene 1 and the hook's evidence use a coded clinic bar chart (two bars per period, First Clinic and Second Clinic, per cent of mothers who died; values from Semmelweis's tables) beside the new chlorinated lime basin plate; the two clinics are text labels only, no rooms, no beds, no people. Scenes 5 to 7 use a coded timeline strip for one measles case (days from infection: incubation, infectious period, rash, isolation, contacts' quarantine window). Scenes 9 and 10 use a coded contact network of about 40 small abstract host circles (grey: can be infected; teal ring: immune; amber: infected), in which an infection spreads along contact lines and stops at teal circles. Scene 11 is a coded four-column criteria table. No people, hands or faces: no doctors, mothers, babies, travellers, patients or health workers; the clinic, the hospital room and the border are shown by objects only (basin, hospital bed, amnesty bin, shipping container, sign). Hands appear in no plate: `m7-handwashing-sink-v1.png` shows the sink and soap only (checked). Coded elements are abstract only: host circles, the network, the bar chart, timeline strip, the criteria table, arrows, break marks, chips and glosses. Scale: plates of objects are shown at a size that reads, not to one scale, each with its own grey label; the measles virus (about 0.15 µm) only ever appears as its own enlarged plate with a grey tag "drawn far larger than real"; the bacterium and norovirus are not drawn to scale against objects. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
